content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method to study the structure of transformer models by projecting the parameters into the space of the input embeddings. They show that the attention matrices can be described by interaction and transition matrices in embedding space which define how a hidden state (defined in terms of combinations of input embeddings) is transformed by that layer by transforming between embeddings. They use this analysis method to analyze features such as which types of words each attention head specializes in, how the parameters change during finetuning, and how the features learned by ensembles of models with the same parameters/settings connect to each other.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper proposed a very interesting mechanism for analyzing transformer-based language models such as BERT and GPT, and providing an interpretable framework for what these models learn. Importantly, the proposed framework is also input-independent, and can be used to analyze the parameters only without having to pass large numbers of possible inputs through the model to analyze the hidden states. Deep neural models are often criticized for their lack of interpretability, and the contributions of this paper provide useful tools for analyzing one of the most common classes of models currently in use. The examples shown are interesting and relevant, and demonstrate that this method can provide valuable insight into what each component of the model learns. 

While I think this paper is very interesting and well-supported, I do think there are a few areas in which it could be improved. First, the proposed analysis method is mostly used to analyze relatively simple features of the layers or hidden states - the top-k most attended to words and the top-k words each of those words is transformed into. The analysis focuses largely on identifying e.g. which types of words each attention head attends most to, or what types of words tend to become the focus after finetuning. This analysis doesn't shed much light into the higher level structure and logic learned by the transformer, and thus there is a limit to its utility. This is, admittedly, a much more difficult problem, however, and I still believe the proposed framework is interesting and useful.
My second criticism would be that the paper primarily focuses on the proposed theoretical framework and examples of how it can be used to make these models more interpretable, and provides little in the way of concrete applications. It would be nice to see some more examples of how this theoretical framework can be used to achieve practical empirical results - see the experiments in Geva et al for toxic language suppression or early exiting, for example.
The one concrete application that this paper does discuss is 'stitching' - performing a zero shot mapping from the latent space of a given model A at a particular intermediate layer to the latent space of model B at some other intermediate layer. While this idea is very interesting, it is discussed only briefly and the results shown are not particularly convincing. If this is section is to be retained, it should be expanded, add justifications for why and how this can be used, and should have more work put into improving the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work is clear, well-written and easy to follow. My one criticism would be that most of the actual results are contained within the appendices - but this is perhaps unavoidable in some areas to avoid cluttering the main paper too much.
The work draws very heavily on the works of Elhage et al (2021) and Geva et al (2022), but it does add significant and novel extensions to the analysis in those works.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the framework proposed by the paper is quite interesting and I recommend it be accepted. While their framework relies on a number of significant assumptions, these assumptions are well justified in the text and examples are given to clearly show the utility of the proposed method. I do think that the proposed method of analysis is limited in some senses as the given examples mostly show simple concepts like the general topics each attention head most closely attends to rather than understanding the higher level structure and logic behind how the model understands language, but this is obviously a much more difficult problem to solve. My hope would be that this method could provide a foundation on which future work could be built to delve deeper into how and what transformers learn. I do also wish that the paper showed some more empirical examples of how their framework could be used to improve model performance or solve concrete problems, but I do not believe this is a significant enough omission to hold it back entirely.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a data-independent method to interpret transformer-based models, by projecting them on the embedding space, i.e. the space of vocabulary items. The authors derive a theoretical framework and provide evidence to support their argument. The authors present two applications for their framework and conduct experiments on the pre-trained GPT-2 model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strong points:**

1. The proposed method to interpret transformers is simple and easy to apply to other pre-trained language models. 

2. The paper is well-written with illustrative figures.

**Weak points:**

*Experiments*

1. The pre-trained model used for the experiments is only GPT-2, which is not diverse. The author‘s justification for excluding layernorm from their analysis in section 4.2 is not convincing to me, since this is only verified for the case of GPT-2.

2. There is a lack of comparison with other data-independent methods in interpreting Transformers.

*Method*
  
1. The work is an extension of [ Elhage et al. [2021]] by adjusting their tools for interpreting self-attention and applied them on pretrained transformer models. The extension is not significant.

2. Assumptions in the paper need to be verified.

      i) The authors state: “When training Transformers with a language modeling objective, the same embedding matrix E is often used [Press and Wolf, 2016] to take the output of the last Transformer layer and project it back to the vocabulary dimension, i.e., into the embedding space”. I do not think this is the state-of-the-art practice in training language modeling with transformers.

      ii) The authors state: “Since the output of the attention module is added to the residual stream, we can assume according to the residual stream view that it is meaningful to project it to the embedding space, similar to FF values”. This statement assumes that the output of each transformer layer is insignificantly updated, and the space of the output tokens at each intermediate layer is still closed to the embeddings states. There is no evidence for this statement.

      iii) The paper uses E’ = E^T only when E is an orthonormal matrix, which is a strong assumption to me.

      iv) As far as I understand, the proposed method can not be applied to many other transformer models trained with different modalities since those do not support standard “vocabulary”. I failed to see that the authors have acknowledged this in their paper, despite their claim that “In this work, we present a theoretical analysis where all parameters of a trained Transformer are interpreted by projecting them into the embedding space, that is, the space of vocabulary items they operate on”.

*Objectives of the paper:*

1. The author points out the downsides of input-dependent interpretation that the example (data points) used for interpretation are not representative of the datasets. To some extent, I agree. However, the paper did not point that whether we can overcome this downside by simply taking the statistics of the interpretation measure over the datasets.

2. The author claims that running input through the model is exhausted. But this reason is not convincing to me since we have to run the data through the model to get the prediction nevertheless. 

**Additional Concerns and Questions for the Authors:**

1. Could the authors please provide more insights and evidence why projecting “hidden states” to the “embedding space” is meaningful? Please address the assumption “Since the output of the attention module is added to the residual stream, we can assume according to the residual stream view that it is meaningful to project it to the embedding space, similar to FF values”.

2. What insights of the pre-trained transformers models that can only be shown via your method but not other data-independent or data-dependent interpretation methods?

**References:**

[1] N. Elhage, N. Nanda, C. Olsson, T. Henighan, N. Joseph, B. Mann, A. Askell, Y. Bai, A. Chen, T. Conerly, N. DasSarma, D. Drain, D. Ganguli, Z. Hatfield-Dodds, D. Hernandez, A. Jones, J. Kernion, L. Lovitt, K. Ndousse, D. Amodei, T. Brown, J. Clark, J. Kaplan, S. McCandlish, and C. Olah. A mathematical framework for transformer circuits, 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written. The quality and novelty of the paper are not high. The details on the experiment settings are useful, but there is no submitted code to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I vote for rejecting. I have three major concerns. First, the proposed interpretation of the transformer is not novel since it is an extension of [Elhage et al. 2021] and does not introduce enough novelty. Second, there is a significant lack of evidence for the strong assumptions made by the authors. Third, experiments with different models are missing, and there is no comparison with other interpretation methods.

content.title: Reply to JdEg
content.comment:
We couldn't quote most of the questions to accommodate our reply.

*Experiments*
1. We thank the reviewer for the comment. Regarding layer normalization, we follow Elhage et al. (2021): “up to a variable scaling, layer norm can be merged into adjacent weights.”  Variable scaling only affects the magnitude of the hidden state and not its vector direction. 
Regarding diversity, we accept the remark. We made the choice of GPT-2 more explicit throughout the paper, leaving other models to future work. We believe that the results will not vary wildly, but the remark is well taken.
Also, we add GPT-2 large examples as well to hint at the applicability of our method in future work.

*Method*
1. Elhage et al. used methods that did not allow them to extend beyond two layers of attention only. Their method failed to work for MLPs as well (a fact stated in their paper). While our method, as is often the case, seems to be trivial in hindsight, the details are of special importance – using the pseudo-inverse instead of E^T would have led to poor outcomes (see answer to 2 for more details), and without carefully designed experiments the method could not be well justified beyond anecdotal observation. 
We think that our work bears only superficial resemblance to Elhage et al, and our starting point is just Geva et al. Indeed, we were made aware of Elhage et al only at a relatively late stage of our work.

2. i) Thank you, we now made the claim explicitly about GPT-2. It is important to note that it does not affect anything in the paper because we are always referring to the output embedding. As a side note, it is worth mentioning that many other architectures use some sort of “weak embedding tying”, where the matrices are tied but the output embedding is preceded by a d x d transformation matrix (this constrains the “effective output embedding”, the transformation+tied embedding, to be a matrix with the same image as the tied embedding matrix).
ii) This is the core of the residual stream view that has been demonstrated extensively (Geva et al, 2020, 2022; Elhage et al. 2021, inter alia) and is our work’s starting point. It's a central component in the modern mechanistic interpretability theory and we simply use it. We refer to the original post: “Interpreting GPT: the logits len” (2019) https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/AcKRB8wDpdaN6v6ru/interpreting-gpt-the-logit-lens

iii) While we did not have space in the main paper, we empirically show in Appendix A that the approximation E’ = E^T is a good approximation when used in combination with the top-k(*) operator for interpretability, we rely on the concept of “top-k robust inverse”: 
$\textrm{keep-k}(xE)^T \textrm{keep-k}(E’ y) \approx x^T y$, where $\textrm{keep-k}(\cdot)$ keeps the top k (in absolute value) coordinates and zeros all the others. It turns out that for small values of k, E’=E^T is better than the pseudo-inverse. For clarity, we will expand a bit on this finding in the main paper for the final version of the paper.

iv) You are indeed correct. The work refers specifically to NLP transformers and we look forward to possible extensions to other domains as well.

*Objectives of the paper*:

1. [...]. However, the paper did not point that whether we can overcome this downside by simply taking the statistics of the interpretation measure over the datasets.

This suggestion requires a lot of compute, running the model on a lot of data. Additionally, we contend that input-independent interpretation is a desirable property regardless. It allows one to locate the origin of certain behaviors of the model. Our method also can be applied to any parameter individually without the rest. With future improvements, it could potentially allow us to enumerate *all* transformer phenomena, rather than try to explain a *specific* phenomenon. 

2. The author claims that running input through the model is exhausted. But this reason is not convincing to me since we have to run the data through the model to get the prediction nevertheless.

On this point, we respectfully disagree with the reviewer. Our approach does not require running inputs through the model at all. We run inputs through the model only in one section of the paper (Section 4.2) to show that our approach indeed correlates with prior work that requires a forward pass.

*Additional Concerns and Questions for the Authors*:

* What insights of the pre-trained transformers models that can only be shown via your method but not other data-independent or data-dependent interpretation methods?

Good question, and amenable to further research. Bear in mind that its main purposes: i) saving computation. ii) Providing mechanistic explanations for the operation of the model. iii) as an example of the latter, we can think of this method as a first order approximation for the “purpose” of a certain *specific* parameter. Also, we use the method to project parameters to a universal space, where different models or seeds can communicate.

content.title: Response to the Author's Rebuttal
content.comment:
Dear authors,

Thank you very much for the answers to my questions! I appreciate your responses, but they do not fully resolve my concerns.

I still lean on the side of rejection because 1) only GPT2 is studied as an example in this paper, 2) it is still not very clear to me that the extension from [ Elhage et al. [2021]]  is significant, and 3) comparisons to data-independent or data-dependent interpretation methods are lacking. 

I keep my score of 3. Nevertheless, I think this is an interesting research direction and will look forward to any updates and future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper attempts to analyze transformers in embedding space. 

In particular, this paper extends the approach in the existing work of Elhage et al. [2021] to project the parameters of a transformer into an embedding space.

This is done by multiplying the parameters by the embedding matrix in the transformer. To project the embeddings back to the parameter space, the paper uses the transpose of the embedding matrix to approximate its right inverse.

Empirically, examine the top-k pairs of vocabulary items for the parameters (e.g., heads) and latent space in a GPT-2 model. It also presents some interpretation of the fine-tuning process. 

Finally, the paper shows that it can align the embedding space of different models and show zero-shot stitching results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1. The problem is important and interesting.   

**Weakness**

1. As mentioned in its main text, the paper's main contribution is to extend the prior work of Elhage et al. [2021] from 2-layer models to multi-layer models. However, it is not clear whether it is technically nontrivial. I did not understand why the parameters in a multi-layer model could not be projected into embedding space.

2. To project the embeddings back to the parameter space, the paper uses the transpose of the embedding matrix as an approximation of its right inverse. How accurate the approximation is?

3. The paper claims that it presents a theoretical analysis. However, I did not see a precise statement and proof of the "theory" in the paper.

4. The results in Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 are not that surprising to me. In fact, it is expected that the well-trained transformers can learn semantic information in its parameters and that different layers in the model serve different roles while two models on the same task may have corresponding modules. Similar things have been investigated in other neural networks and shallow transformers. Are there any new insights that we can obtain from the interpretation? 

5. Sec. 4 only considers GPT-2 as an example to validate the proposed method. It is better to analyze more models (e.g., with different model sizes or trained on different datasets) to draw a conclusion.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the clarity of the paper should be significantly improved. A standard machine learning paper should treat "theory" more seriously. In particular, please at least present and prove your theory rigorously such that readers can understand what's your theory and check the proof.

Quality & Novelty: the paper did not emphasize the technical challenge of extending the prior work of Elhage et al. [2021] from 2-layer models to multi-layer models and I did not get it either. So the significance and novelty are limited.

Reproducibility: it seems reproducible to me.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer jfFa
content.comment:
1. As mentioned in its main text, the paper's main contribution is to extend the prior work of Elhage et al. [2021] from 2-layer models to multi-layer models. However, it is not clear whether it is technically nontrivial. I did not understand why the parameters in a multi-layer model could not be projected into embedding space.

Thank you for this comment. Elhage et al. used methods that did not allow them to extend beyond two layers of attention only. Their method failed to work for MLPs as well (a fact stated in their paper). While our method, as is often the case, seems to be trivial in hindsight, the details are of special importance – using the pseudo-inverse instead of E^T would have led to poor outcomes (see answer to 2 for more details), and without carefully designed experiments the method could not be well justified beyond anecdotal observation. 
We think that our work bears only superficial resemblance to Elhage et al, and our starting point is just Geva et al. Indeed, we were made aware of Elhage et al only at a relatively late stage of our work.

2. To project the embeddings back to the parameter space, the paper uses the transpose of the embedding matrix as an approximation of its right inverse. How accurate the approximation is?

While we did not have space in the main paper, we empirically show in Appendix A that the approximation E’ = E^T is a good approximation when used in combination with the top-k(*) operator for interpretability, we rely on the concept of “top-k robust inverse”: 
$\textrm{keep-k}(xE)^T \textrm{keep-k}(E’ y) \approx x^T y$, where $\textrm{keep-k}(\cdot)$ keeps the top k (in absolute value) coordinates and zeros all the others. It turns out that for small values of k, E’=E^T is better than the pseudo-inverse. For clarity, we will expand a bit on this finding in the main paper for the final version of the paper.

3. The paper claims that it presents a theoretical analysis. However, I did not see a precise statement and proof of the "theory" in the paper.

We agree the terminology might not be optimal. When we discuss “theoretical analysis” we refer to the “derivation” section (Sec. 3). In the new version of the paper we refer to this as “conceptual framework”. Indeed, our derivation relies on simple mathematical notions, but the conceptual framework that interprets them relies on strong assumptions that must be verified and that’s the purpose of the paper. We thank the reviewers for pointing out this misnomer and apply the relevant changes to the paper.

4. The results in Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 are not that surprising to me. In fact, it is expected that the well-trained transformers can learn semantic information in its parameters and that different layers in the model serve different roles while two models on the same task may have corresponding modules. [....]

The experiments are designed to prove, either directly (mostly Sec. 4) or consequentially (mostly Sec. 5) that the above projections are indeed the correct way of interpreting parameters in embedding space. Indeed, if one assumes the above postulates to be true, they are derivable rigorously from them. If one, on the other hand, expects the postulates to be wrong the experiments are improbable and surprising. 

5. Sec. 4 only considers GPT-2 as an example to validate the proposed method. It is better to analyze more models (e.g., with different model sizes or trained on different datasets) to draw a conclusion.

We accept the remark. We made the choice of GPT-2 more explicit throughout the paper, leaving other models to future work. We believe that the results will not vary wildly, but the remark is well taken.
Also, we add GPT-2 large examples as well to hint at the applicability of our method in future work.

Regarding originality:
* Unifying Geva and Elhage, and stating the expected structure of embedding space projection of all parameters - using the right inverse. 
* We explain the surprising effectiveness of E^T and not pseudo-inverse using the surprising observation of the behavior of “keep-k robustness".
* Carefully designing experiments to support the derivation, that relies on postulates otherwise too strong to take for granted
* Using the embedding space as a means of communication for models, is a unique take that was not used before.

Also, in terms of plain novelty (as opposed to pure originality of idea), it allows for new possibilities in the future:
* All parameters of real world transformers can be readily interpreted. No single work we are aware of has offered such a possibility. 
* In the future, a possible outcome might be taking a Transformer and converting it to one that works explicitly in the embedding space.
* We present, for the first time to our knowledge, *zero-shot* stitching between models.

We humbly ask the reviewer to re-evaluate their score. Regardless, we thank them for their time and effort and would be pleased to provide further clarification if necessary.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an approach to interpreting transformer weights in embedding space via projections.  The authors build on top of previous observations that the prediction is determined in the early layers of a transformer and do not change much in later layers and use this to justify directly projecting hidden states in every layer into embedding space.  Then the embedding projections for different layer types within the transformer architecture  are derived along with an approximate projection substituting the transpose of the embedding matrix for its inverse.  Then, we see three applications of the embedding view of transformer weights: (1) interpreting weights for pre-trained and fine-tuned transformers, (2) aligning weights of transformers trained with different seeds  over the same vocabulary, and (3) creating a new classifier without training that combines a fine-tuned head from one model with a pre-trained body from another by translation weights in embedding space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The authors introduce an empirically validated view of transformer weights in embedding space.
- The 3 applications demonstrate a convincing level of evidence for thinking about transformers in embedding space instead of feature space.

Cons:
- There are some strong assumptions made for the approximate projections which are used from the empirical studies.  In particular, that we can project directly to embedding space, use transpose of the embedding matrix instead of the inverse, and ignore normalization layers.  
- While interesting, the applications do not seem useful in practice (parameter interpretation or alignment) nor reliable enough (zero-shot stitching).  
- The embedding view for the predictions has been studied previously by Geva et al., 2022 as noted by the authors.
- If the goal is interpretability, it's not too satisfying to get a flat interpretation instead of a sequence of modifications made via a path through the network as we saw with the work by Ehlage et al. 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
The paper is well written overall.
## Quality
The authors provide empirical support for their approach to analyzing transformers in embedding space but there are still a few missing pieces for the insights to be more robust/reliable and useful.
## Novelty
Viewing the predictions in embedding space is not a new idea but extending it to all the layers of the transformer is a novel concept.
## Reproducibility
The experiments are pretty straightforward but it is unclear whether the attention heads and examples in the appendix are representative or a heavily filtered set.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting view of interpreting all weights of transformers in embedding space and empirically validate the proposed projections.  I do believe the idea would be of value for the research community but I think the work can be fleshed out more to address some of the limitations/assumptions and/or provide more well motivated uses for the embedding-based view of interpreting transformers.

* There are some strong assumptions made for the approximate projections which are used from the empirical studies. In particular, that we can project directly to embedding space, use transpose of the embedding matrix instead of the inverse, and ignore normalization layers.

Thank you for this comment. While we did not have space in the main paper, we empirically show in Appendix A that the approximation E’ = E^T is a good approximation when used in combination with the top-k(*) operator for interpretability, we rely on the concept of “top-k robust inverse”: 
$\textrm{keep-k}(xE)^T \textrm{keep-k}(E’ y) \approx x^T y$, where $\textrm{keep-k}(\cdot)$ keeps the top k (in absolute value) coordinates and zeros all the others. It turns out that for small values of k, E’=E^T is better than the pseudo-inverse. For clarity, we will expand a bit on this finding in the main paper for the final version of the paper.

We follow Elhage et al. (2021) regarding layer normalization: “up to a variable scaling, layer norm can be merged into adjacent weights.”  Variable scaling only affects the magnitude of the hidden state and not its vector direction.

* While interesting, the applications do not seem useful in practice (parameter interpretation or alignment) nor reliable enough (zero-shot stitching).

We humbly accept these claims but we wish to think of this work as a proof of concept, which provides evidence for the validity of our framework for future work in interpretability. The purpose of the applications is to serve as further indirect evidence for the appropriateness of our framework to boost confidence in our system. For the purpose of conciseness, we designed a set of experiments that would serve this main goal.
